vignette:
Mikaele, a 67-year-old interior designer, sat hunched forward, his hands clasped tightly, the years of his life etched into the lines around his eyes. He had been a vibrant, sought-after professional, known for his keen eye and warm demeanour, but that life felt like a distant memory since his ordeal years ago. He had been on a design consultation trip abroad, working on a boutique hotel project, when he was unexpectedly seized by armed individuals and held captive for several harrowing days. The memory of the small, suffocating room, the rough burlap sack over his head, and the guttural shouts in Arabic that punctuated the terrifying silence, remained vivid and visceral. He still heard those voices in his head sometimes when he had memories of what happened, making the past feel terrifyingly present.

In the years that followed, Mikaele found himself increasingly struggling. Any sudden, intrusive memory of the event, particularly the feeling of being trapped or the echo of those angry voices, would plunge him into an immediate, overwhelming sense of fear and horror. This sense of threat was profound; he often felt his body react to danger before his mind had even had time to think, his heart racing and breath catching. This pervasive alertness meant that even the slightest hint of a confined space or a muffled sound could instantly register as a direct threat, activating his memories of the captivity. This made him feel unsafe unless his back was against a wall where he could see the entire room, a subtle but constant vigilance that became exhausting. As a result, Mikaele began to employ a series of maladaptive strategies to cope. He started avoiding enclosed or confined spaces, which presented a significant challenge for an interior designer whose work often involved small client offices, confined material libraries, or even just sitting across a desk from someone.

The pervasive sense of threat further complicated his relationship with his own memories. When he tried to explain what had happened to him, he would often lose the thread and simply couldn't finish, the words getting stuck, leaving him feeling frustrated and isolated. Sometimes, when the memories did surface, he could recall what happened but felt completely numb, as if it had happened to a stranger, a detachment that offered a strange, unsettling protection from the overwhelming negative emotions. These fragmented and emotionally distant memories, however, did little to alleviate his underlying sense of danger; in fact, they often intensified his feeling that he was still in peril, that the world was an unsafe place.

His maladaptive strategies, while offering fleeting relief, ultimately tightened the grip of his distress. His avoidance of work or study, initially a way to prevent encountering triggers, became a self-perpetuating cycle. Client meetings became impossible to manage, as the small offices or conference rooms would immediately trigger his fear of enclosed spaces, sending his anxiety soaring. He had to withdraw from several ongoing projects, and his once-thriving business dwindled. To manage social interactions, Mikaele would rehearse what to say before any interaction, fearing that feeling emotionally vulnerable might expose him to some undefined danger. This intense focus on controlling his external presentation inadvertently made his internal recollections feel even more distant and disjointed, as if the genuine memory was something he had to continually suppress rather than integrate. This constant mental preparation, however, made his conversations stilted and artificial, further isolating him and reinforcing his belief that he was inherently unsafe, leading to persistent negative emotions like shame and anger at his situation. The very strategies he used to feel safe paradoxically maintained his profound sense of threat, making him even more susceptible to triggers. He had come to believe that if he ever let his guard down, even for a moment, the danger would resurface.

Now, a widower living alone, Mikaele found the tight, self-reinforcing loops of his symptoms unbearable. The constant vigilance, the gnawing fear, and the profound isolation had become his daily reality. He finally sought help, desperately hoping to find a way out of the suffocating cage his life had become, but terrified that any attempt to confront his past would only bring back the horror he had fought so hard to contain.
